questions.question: What are “Black Swans”?

options.text: Frequent events with predictable and minor impacts.
Outlier events that often have extreme and unpredictable impacts.
Known risks that are intentionally ignored during model training.
Events that follow a thin-tailed distribution and have negligible consequences.

questions.explanation: Robustness Part 1 [3:36-5:12] - Black swans are events that are outliers, lying outside typical expectations, and often carry extreme impact.

questions.question: Which of the following is considered a “Known Unknown”? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Recollection
Closed-ended Questions
Meta-ignorance
Conscious Ignorance
Open-ended Exploration
Self-analysis

questions.explanation: Robustness Part 1 [19:20-22:05] - “Known Unknowns” are things we are aware of but don’t understand such as known classic risks/conscious ignorance or closed-ended questions.

questions.question: Which type of distribution shift occurs when the input distribution changes between 𝑃(𝑥) training and testing but remains constant? 𝑃(𝑦|𝑥)

options.text: Concept shift
Normalized shift
Covariate shift
Prior probability shift

questions.explanation: Robustness Part 2 [23:00-24:53] - P(x) changes between train and test, but p(y|x) does not change in covariate shift.

questions.question: What is “transferability” in the context of adversarial attacks?

options.text: The ability to move a model from a secure state to a vulnerable state.
The phenomenon where adversarial examples crafted for one model also fool another model.
Converting a black-box model into a white-box model.
The process of retraining a model on adversarial attacks.

questions.explanation: Lecture 8 and 9 Lecture Notes (Slide 70): Adversarial examples crafted for one model, can be used to attack other models is known as transferability.

questions.question: According to the lecture, what is a common trade-off when using Adversarial Training to improve robustness?

options.text: It requires a significantly larger dataset than normal training.
It can significantly reduce the accuracy on clean examples.
It only works for simple binary classifiers.
It requires a low-variance dataset to function effectively.

questions.explanation: Lecture 8 and 9 Lecture Notes (Slide 78): Currently, adversarial training can reduce accuracy on clean examples by 10%+.

questions.question: Which of the following are challenges associated with direct human ratings when modeling preferences? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Human-in-the-loop evaluation is expensive and time-consuming.
Direct ratings require white-box access to the model.
Human ratings are always completely objective and free from annotator bias.
Human judgments are noisy and miscalibrated.

questions.explanation: RLHF [8:39-13:31] - There are two problems with human ratings: human-in-the-loop is expensive and human judgments are noisy and miscalibrated.

questions.question: What does Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) represent in the RLHF framework?

options.text: RLHF without the reward model
RLHF without human feedback
RLHF without reinforcement learning
RLHF without policy optimization

questions.explanation: AI Alignment [4:54-6:35] - RLHF – Reward model = Direct Preference Optimization (DPO)

questions.question: What is the first step of the RLHF pipeline?

options.text: Collecting comparison data and training a reward model.
Optimizing a policy against the reward model using reinforcement learning.
Collecting demonstration data and training a supervised policy.
Performing external white-box auditing of the pretrained model.

questions.explanation: RLHF [3:57-6:38] - The first step in the RLHF pipeline is to collect demonstration data and train a supervised model.

questions.question: Why is black-box access insufficient for rigorous AI audits?

options.text: It is too expensive for external auditors.
It does not allow for human-in-the-loop feedback.
It prevents the use of reinforcement learning.
It only allows auditors to query the system and observe outputs.

questions.explanation: AI Alignment [24:28-25:13] - Auditors can only query the system and observe its output.

questions.question: According to the lecture, what does the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence penalty prevent in RLHF?

options.text: The reward model from becoming too complex
The policy model from diverging too far from the initial pretrained model
Human evaluators from providing biased feedback
The model from over-generalizing

questions.explanation: RLHF [14:31-16:35] - Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence is the penalty which prevents us from diverging too far from the pretrained model.

questions.question: Which of the following is true? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Extremistan has thin tails while Medicristan has long tails.
Extremistan is determined by many small events.
Mediocristan is the tyranny of the collective.
Extremistan’s impact is potentially scalable.

questions.question: Identify the equations that can lead to a long-tailed distribution.

options.text: Idea * student * resources * time
Idea * student + resources * time
Idea + student + resource + time
Idea - student * resource - time

questions.explanation: Robustness Part 1 [15:17-17:21] - Research output = Ideas X Time X Students X Resources
